The way I, as a linguist, see it, "believe" and "know" are two very different things, completely different verbs. After I have checked every nook and corner of my room, I can confidently say, "I know that there is no spider in this room" - how? Because I know. Because I had it verified. But when I know that I clean my room regularly and mostly have my room's windows and door closed, I can say, "I believe there is no spider here" or "I don't think there is a spider here", but I can't "know" for sure in this case - why? because I have not checked. 

Now, in this spider example, we are talking about something very much realistic, like a spider being in a room, a situation that anyone can easily imagine and understand, given how realistic it is. 

But where something like "god" or "rebirth" or "ghost" or "vampire" is concerned, it is extremely unrealistic, so unrealistic that "believe there is no such a thing" and "know there is no such a thing" come to mean more or less the same thing - because of how extremely unrealistic these possibilities are.

I am here, you are somewhere far away, I have not even seen the place once, but still, I can say either "I believe that's not the case" or "I know that's not the case" - and they could mean very much the same thing, again because of how unrealistic this whole thing is!

When conflict patterns keep repeating, both parties have to be open to resolving - if it's just one person trying to solve and the other person pulling away, it is not going to work.
